samples.title: NeuroLens (trailer)
samples.attribution: NeuroLens launch trailer (original work by the NeuroLens team).

report.headline: Face sequences earn the strongest signals. The spinning brain finale loses visual engagement right before the CTA.
report.summary: Close-up animated faces drive the two clearest engagement peaks in the video, and the muted-signal demo confirms the visuals hold up independently. The abstract brain animation runs over 13 seconds without a face, so the visual channel slides below typical through the credibility payoff. Getting a face into the Minutes reveal is the most direct fix.

moments.what_happens: Big Buck Bunny fills the frame as a butterfly lands on its head.
moments.brain_response: Face and body signals reach the video's highest levels here. A close-up animated face with moment-to-moment action is the single strongest visual engagement driver in the whole piece.

moments.what_happens: Labels float onto a black screen naming each brain-signal category.
moments.brain_response: Face and visual channels drop well below typical while audio stays elevated. The section explaining what brain signals measure has nothing human for the brain to actually process visually.
moments.suggestion: Layer each label over a one-second clip that exemplifies that category so the visual channel tracks the concept being introduced.

moments.what_happens: Bunny close-up in garden; on-screen graph shows with-sound vs muted comparison.
moments.brain_response: The muted prediction tracks slightly above the with-sound prediction throughout this stretch, confirming the visual storytelling carries the scene on its own. The product demo works exactly as claimed.

moments.what_happens: Spinning brain model holds while text reveals the brain-scan credibility claim and Minutes payoff.
moments.brain_response: Visual and face channels slide steadily below typical across all 13 seconds, running in the opposite direction from the story's climactic beat. No face means nothing for the visual brain to anchor to.
moments.suggestion: Cut to a character or human face reacting as the Minutes counter completes. Even two seconds of a face landing on the result would hold the visual channel through the close.

strengths: The hooked-versus-drift bunny sequence is the video's engagement peak, making the product concept tangible rather than abstract.
The side-by-side opening comparison sustains well-above-typical engagement longer than any other single segment, with Sintel's face doing heavy visual lifting.
improvements: The spinning brain model holds the frame for over 13 seconds at the end, so visual engagement falls well below typical exactly when viewers should be most committed to acting.
The sub-signals label reveal is the one place where story and brain arc pull apart most: the topic is brain signals, but there is nothing human on screen for the brain to process.

samples.title: Swee Choon (TikTok)
samples.attribution: © Swee Choon Tim Sum (TikTok). Shown for non-commercial analysis.

report.headline: Opening hook builds well, but the problem setup and tower CTA drop the face anchor at the wrong moments
report.summary: The story premise and back alley reveal both earn strong brain responses, with the reveal hitting the highest body signal in the video. The problem-confession section loses almost all visual engagement and leans entirely on spoken words, and the drink tower unlock shot cuts away from her face right when the reward needs to land. Fix both by keeping her physically in the frame during those two beats.

moments.what_happens: She holds up hall and midnight madness posters, declaring the task out loud.
moments.brain_response: Overall climbs through its first sustained high. Faces, bodies, and scenes all rise together as the story premise locks in for the viewer.

moments.what_happens: Black-and-white footage and old photos illustrate the golden era of hall nights.
moments.brain_response: Scenes signal peaks at its highest point here, and overall stays well above typical. With sound off, engagement falls to near zero, meaning the nostalgia payoff is almost entirely word-driven.
moments.suggestion: Cut in one second of her reacting to the photos to give the visual track a face anchor that holds without the narration.

moments.what_happens: A text card introduces the problem, then she confesses in selfie-cam that Gen Z doesn't know the venue.
moments.brain_response: Visual and scenes signals drop from their earlier highs. With sound off, engagement is essentially zero, so this whole beat lives on her words alone.
moments.suggestion: Open on her standing in the empty back alley instead of a text card, so the location does visual work independent of the narration.

moments.what_happens: Back alley reveal with her arms wide open, delivering the boss's command to fill it.
moments.brain_response: Bodies signal hits its highest point in the entire video. The redesigned venue and her physicality together hold the visual even without sound, the clearest sign a creative choice fully paid off.

moments.what_happens: Red-arrow graphic points at the drink tower reward with no presenter face visible.
moments.brain_response: Faces drop to their lowest in the CTA section. At the exact moment she names the key reward, the visual loses the human anchor that drove engagement throughout.
moments.suggestion: Keep her beside the tower in a two-shot so her reaction lands with the prop, rather than cutting to the prop alone.

strengths: The intern-on-a-mission framing builds consistently across the first half, with seeing, hearing, and understanding all climbing together rather than competing.
The back alley reveal earns the video's highest body signal, confirming that putting her physically inside the redesigned space was the right directorial call.
improvements: The problem-setup stretch is the most sound-dependent passage in the video. Grounding it visually in the actual empty venue would give it weight even on mute.
The CTA loses the face presence that made the first half work. Staying on her face through the reward announcement would carry the momentum into the DM ask.

samples.title: YouTrip (TikTok)
samples.attribution: © YouTrip Singapore (TikTok). Shown for non-commercial analysis.

report.headline: Office tour earns the video's best attention; the CTA loses the job-stakes story too early
report.summary: The physical absurdity of the office tour and the well-timed 'I almost forgot' pivot into the ad are both genuinely effective, with the brain signals to back them up. From the locker-room CTA onward the story hook disappears and speech and social engagement fall below typical viewing levels, leaving the 'boss will fire me' punchline to land after attention has already drifted. Tying the job-stakes back into the CTA delivery would hold the audience through to the end.

moments.what_happens: Camera whips to a colleague holding umbrellas up to the ceiling.
moments.brain_response: Bodies signal hits its highest point in the entire video across these two seconds. The physical absurdity of someone doing something unexpected overhead locks visual attention in a way no talking-head shot in the video matches.

moments.what_happens: She turns back to camera with 'I almost forgot, my boss wants me to tell you something very important.'
moments.brain_response: Speech and social engagement peak here, the strongest understanding response in the video. Framing the product reveal as a personal secret she nearly missed makes the brain treat it as story information, not advertising.

moments.what_happens: Branded YouTrip screen fills the background as she delivers the giveaway details.
moments.brain_response: Understanding is still elevated but falling steadily, and visual engagement drops as the graphic takes over the frame. The face signal weakens when the screen competes with her for attention.
moments.suggestion: Crop tighter on her face during the reveal and let the branded graphic appear as a small insert; her expression selling the prize keeps faces and social engagement higher than the screen can.

moments.what_happens: She moves to the locker room and begins explaining the entry mechanic.
moments.brain_response: Speech and social drop to near or below typical viewing levels. The 'intern getting hired' story thread has been set down completely, and the brain registers the shift to straight product delivery.
moments.suggestion: Bring the job stakes back into the entry mechanic: frame spending $400 as 'one more way you can help me keep my job' to stay inside the story rather than stepping outside it for the terms.

moments.what_happens: She delivers the closing line: 'If you don't listen to me, my boss is going to fire me.'
moments.brain_response: The callback arrives after speech and social have been sliding for roughly ten seconds, so it registers in an already quieter brain state. The comedic payoff needs attention to land.
moments.suggestion: Move this line immediately after the entry mechanic, before listing the deadline, so the story punchline closes the sell rather than following it.

strengths: Rotating through distinct office locations with physical props (giant card, bean bags, umbrella colleague) drives the highest bodies and visual engagement in the video and keeps the tour feeling alive.
The 'I almost forgot' device is an effective editorial tool here, it reactivates social attention and frames the sponsored message as a story beat the presenter personally owes the viewer.
improvements: With the sound off, visual engagement is below typical for most of the video, meaning the content depends heavily on the voice carrying it; adding more physical action or props in the CTA section would give the visuals more independent weight.

The closing callback to the job-stakes story comes too late to lift the final impression; building that thread into the CTA itself would let the comedy and the product information work together instead of in sequence.

samples.title: McDonald’s x G-Dragon (TikTok)
samples.attribution: © McDonald’s Singapore (TikTok). Shown for non-commercial analysis.

report.headline: Fan photo moment is your strongest beat; people need to stay in frame through the interior tour
report.summary: The opening and fan-interaction sequence earn genuinely above-typical engagement, driven by faces and bodies on screen. Once the camera moves inside without people, the brain's response slides steadily through the back half and the CTA lands when attention is already fading. Put someone in the interior shots and lead the CTA with a person, not a logo close-up.

moments.what_happens: Camera reveals the MCG heart floor graphic then the full decorated interior wall.
moments.brain_response: Scenes signal is climbing and overall is well above typical. The environment is visually novel and dense with branding, pulling the viewer through the reveal.

moments.what_happens: Two people pose and laugh with the G-Dragon cardboard standee outside.
moments.brain_response: Bodies signal hits its highest point in the whole video here, with faces strong too. The human playfulness in front of the branded standee is what earns that peak, not the decor alone.

moments.what_happens: Night exterior shots show the illuminated McDonald's facade and G-Dragon door mural.
moments.brain_response: Scenes signal actually peaks here as the lit-up exterior is striking, but faces and bodies have dropped away, so overall engagement is sliding toward typical. The environment is doing all the work.
moments.suggestion: Cut one of the night exterior wide shots and replace with a quick clip of people reacting to the glow outside, so bodies stay in the mix.

moments.what_happens: Interior wall slogans, merchandise display, and dining area shots with no main subject on camera.
moments.brain_response: Overall dips to near or below typical. Without people in frame, the brain is reading a scene rather than a story, and faces and bodies signals drop close to or under zero.
moments.suggestion: Walk someone through these shots, pointing at the merch or reading the wall, to keep the social layer alive through the interior segment.

moments.what_happens: Close-up of glowing golden arches with the CTA text on screen.
moments.brain_response: Engagement is already well below typical before this card appears, meaning the audience has mentally checked out before the call to action arrives.
moments.suggestion: Move the CTA closer to t=20 while energy still exists, or open it with the fan-photo payoff image so it feels like an invitation rather than a sign-off.

strengths: The fan interaction sequence (posing, laughing, filming each other) gives the video a genuine human story that the brain tracks better than any decor shot alone.
The visual environment stays consistently above typical for most of the video, showing the branded space is strong enough to hold attention even when pacing slows.
improvements: The back half loses its human element entirely; keeping at least one person on camera through the interior tour would prevent the steady slide in engagement after t=10.
The CTA arrives at the video's weakest point; anchoring it to a moment of fan excitement rather than a logo close-up would give it real momentum.

report.headline: Bodies and faces carry the comedy, but the boardroom section costs the ad its visual momentum before the final punchline lands
report.summary: The massage sequence and two-face close-up drive the strongest brain response in the spot, with the bodies signal hitting its absolute peak there and carrying the absurdist premise perfectly. The boardroom presentation runs about four seconds past its usefulness, as overall engagement steadily thins while the wide shot shrinks every face in frame. A tighter cut through the CeraVe offices would keep the energy up for the final text joke.

moments.what_happens: Cera holds up the CeraVe tub with a deadpan stare.
moments.brain_response: Faces and bodies signals are both climbing fast here, well above typical. The celebrity face plus product in one frame is doing real work for the brain.

moments.what_happens: Michael Cera massages a stranger in a spa tent, then the client's face fills the frame.
moments.brain_response: Bodies signal reaches its highest point in the entire ad, with faces also near their peak. The physical absurdity locks the viewer in more than any dialogue or product shot in the spot.

moments.what_happens: A lone figure rock-climbs a sheer cliff face in an epic wide.
moments.brain_response: Scenes signal rises sharply as bodies hands off some of its load, keeping overall engagement high. The escalation in visual scale sustains the absurdist build without losing momentum.

moments.what_happens: Wide boardroom shot: doctors review Michael Cera's ad footage on a large screen.
moments.brain_response: Overall engagement drops noticeably as the wide frame shrinks every face to a fraction of its earlier size. Social and understanding signals hold up, so the joke registers cognitively, but the visual pull fades.
moments.suggestion: Cut in a closer reaction shot of one or two skeptical dermatologists during this stretch to keep the face-driven energy alive before the product card.

moments.what_happens: Static product shot with the line: Developed with Dermatologists. Not Michael Cera.
moments.brain_response: Understanding and speech signals stay positive while visual goes below typical, meaning the written punchline is being read and processed but the static frame adds no visual energy of its own.
moments.suggestion: Trim one second off the card's hold time so the punchline lands crisply and the ad ends before the visual signal drifts further down.

strengths: The smooth escalation from talking-head to product reveal to full physical absurdity keeps visual engagement above typical for the entire first two-thirds of the ad without a single weak cut.
Two faces in the same frame during the massage payoff is the single best visual decision in the spot, confirmed by the bodies signal peaking there above every other moment.
improvements: The boardroom sequence is four seconds of wide shots where the face-driven energy that powered the first half has nowhere to go; tighter coverage of the room's reactions would fix this.
The final card's understanding signal shows the text joke is working, but staying on a static product shot for three-plus seconds after the punchline is delivered asks the viewer to wait for nothing.

report.headline: The punchline earns a genuine spike but the narwhal scene and final product stretch run longer than the joke can carry them
report.summary: The first 25 seconds are the strongest: face, voice, and the core concept peak together as Michael names himself and claims the cream. The narwhal sequence and closing product-gazing section run below typical in speech engagement, coasting on visuals after the joke is already told. Two targeted cuts would recover the energy.

moments.what_happens: Michael Cera names himself and holds up the cream for the first time.
moments.brain_response: Hearing spikes to its highest point in the entire video as face and voice lock in simultaneously. The reveal is landing exactly as intended.

moments.what_happens: GENEROSITY title card plays over Michael claiming he is CeraVe.
moments.brain_response: Understanding reaches its peak for the whole video and social engagement is also climbing. The joke's conceptual twist is fully registering, not just being heard but processed as a social situation.

moments.what_happens: Wide spa tent shot: Michael gets a massage with the cream jar on the table.
moments.brain_response: Bodies signal peaks at one of its highest readings across the whole video, but understanding and social engagement are well below the earlier comedy sections. The scene looks great but the wit has thinned out.
moments.suggestion: Cut a quick reaction shot of Michael's face mid-massage here to reactivate the face and social signals without breaking the absurdist gag.

moments.what_happens: CGI narwhal surfaces and compliments Michael's skin via subtitle.
moments.brain_response: Visuals and bodies stay above typical but speech understanding drops to its lowest point in the ad. The subtitle-only punchline bypasses the brain's hearing and speech systems entirely.
moments.suggestion: Give the narwhal an actual voice line instead of a subtitle. That one change pulls speech and social engagement back above typical at what should be a peak comedy beat.

moments.what_happens: Michael gazes affectionately at the cream jar during the product claim voiceover.
moments.brain_response: Seeing falls below typical and faces goes negative as the frame locks onto the jar rather than a face. Understanding stays only modestly above typical. The comedic energy has spent itself and this stretch extends past where engagement can hold.
moments.suggestion: Cut two seconds earlier and move straight to the trio finale at around second 67, where multiple faces re-activate the social signal for the brand close.

strengths: The silhouette build from seconds 0 to 9 hands off perfectly to Michael Cera's face reveal, creating a visual ramp that meets the hearing spike right on cue.

Running the absurdist joke across multiple scenarios (spa, rock climb, fantasy garden) keeps bodies and scenes above typical through most of the middle section, sustaining visual momentum even when speech drops.
improvements: The narwhal is the ad's most original visual idea but it fires below typical in speech and social engagement because the punchline lives only in a subtitle.
The closing product section lingers about four seconds after seeing has already dropped below typical; ending sooner on the trio shot would close on a stronger face and social signal.

samples.title: MediShield Life ad (30 s cut)
samples.attribution: © Ministry of Health Singapore. Shown for non-commercial analysis.

report.headline: Crisis scenes grip the brain, but the core promise plays over near-black frames and the resolution lands after momentum has already unwound
report.summary: The hospital drama arc from the gurney rush through the trauma and prosthetic scenes earns the ad's strongest sustained engagement, and the brand tagline holds reasonably well. The two real gaps are a stretch of near-dark frames that coincide exactly with the most important voiceover line, and a resolution hug that arrives after overall engagement has been declining for a few seconds. Fix those two timing issues and the story arc and brain arc run together cleanly.

moments.what_happens: Tight close-up of a mother crying over her sick child.
moments.brain_response: Despite being one of the most charged images in the ad, the face signal barely clears typical and overall sits slightly below. The brain has not had enough scene context yet to process the emotional weight.
moments.suggestion: Give the viewer a wider establishing frame of the hospital room before cutting to her face, so the close-up lands with the full force it earns visually.

moments.what_happens: Near-black transitional frames as the voiceover delivers the brand promise.
moments.brain_response: See and bodies drop to their lowest points in the entire ad, right as the script says the most important line. The visual track goes essentially dark, leaving the promise with nothing to anchor it.
moments.suggestion: Hold a slow push on the child's hand or the mother's face through this line rather than wiping to black. Keep at least one human detail on screen while the promise is spoken.

moments.what_happens: Emergency gurney rushes down a corridor, cutting to a bloody trauma scene and a prosthetic knee brace.
moments.brain_response: Overall peaks here and the bodies signal hits its highest reading of the ad. Physical detail, motion, and medical urgency working together lock the brain in even with the sound removed.

moments.what_happens: Young man in wheelchair walks the corridor, then his mother embraces him in a tearful hug.
moments.brain_response: Engagement is well above typical but noticeably lower than the crisis peak, and the overall signal has been sliding for a couple of seconds before the hug actually lands. The payoff arrives a beat after its own momentum.
moments.suggestion: Cut from the wheelchair push directly to the embrace, trimming the corridor walk by a second, so the hug catches the brain while the signal is still climbing rather than coasting down.

moments.what_happens: Green brand card with the tagline appears.
moments.brain_response: Overall holds above typical through both seconds, carried by the hearing channel as the voiceover reads the lines. The story has deposited enough goodwill for the brand message to register.

strengths: Physical detail shots such as hands, medical equipment, and the prosthetic leg sustain strong visual engagement across varied scenes without depending entirely on face close-ups.
The brand tagline arrives while overall engagement is still above typical, giving the product message a solid emotional platform rather than landing into a cold finish.
improvements: The core brand promise in the voiceover plays over the visually emptiest stretch of the ad. Align a human visual anchor with that line so words and pictures reinforce each other at the most important moment.
The emotional resolution loses momentum before the hug lands. Tightening the corridor sequence by a second or two would let the payoff catch the brain on the upswing rather than the downswing.

samples.title: MediShield Life ad (60 s cut)
samples.attribution: © Ministry of Health Singapore. Shown for non-commercial analysis.

report.headline: The payoff in the final third earns the brand message, but the bill explanation stretch loses ground exactly where the product needs to land
report.summary: This film builds effectively from crisis to recovery, and the final family scenes deliver the strongest balanced engagement in the whole piece. The mid-ad stretch where the bill and MediShield text appear is the quietest moment overall, which is a problem because that is where the product explanation sits. Tightening the dark blurry transitions early on would also recover attention that the story has already earned.

moments.what_happens: Blurry dark corridor frames bridge the hospital room to the emergency sequence.
moments.brain_response: With faces gone and imagery abstracted to near black, seeing, hearing, and understanding all drop below typical together. The viewer has nowhere to anchor.
moments.suggestion: Cut two seconds earlier into the dialysis ward wide shot or stay on the crying mother's face through the voiceover line. Either gives the brain something to hold.

moments.what_happens: Emergency gurney rushes down a corridor, cutting to a bloody injury and worried family.
moments.brain_response: The bodies signal spikes to its highest point in the whole ad as the kinetic action locks in visual attention. But speech and social understanding sit at their lowest here, so the brain is tracking movement without connecting it to the broader story.
moments.suggestion: A single line of voiceover or a brief reaction shot of a family member during this stretch would let understanding catch up to what the visuals are doing.

moments.what_happens: Close-up of a bill on a table with the MediShield Life text explanation on screen.
moments.brain_response: Overall engagement and understanding both reach their softest point in the entire film here. With sound off the response is equally quiet, meaning the visual composition alone is not carrying the scene.
moments.suggestion: Put a human face in frame while the bill is revealed, even as a reflection or background presence. It reconnects the financial message to a person and pulls the face signal back up where the product explanation needs it most.

moments.what_happens: Mother pulls her son into a tight embrace in the hospital corridor at discharge.
moments.brain_response: Engagement holds above typical and, notably, stays above typical even with the sound off. The composition and performance alone are doing the work here without needing the voiceover.

moments.what_happens: Daughter turns back smiling, then parents look up warmly in an outdoor park setting.
moments.brain_response: This is the peak of the whole ad. Seeing, hearing, and understanding are all above typical simultaneously, the only stretch where all three channels align this cleanly. The faces close-up after the logo-backpack cutaway is what tips it over.

strengths: The final family sequence earns the strongest balanced response in the film, with all three brain channels working together, which means the emotional payoff genuinely lands before the tagline arrives.
The discharge hug holds above typical even with the sound turned off, so the visual storytelling in that moment stands on its own without relying on music or voice.
improvements: The bill close-up is where understanding dips furthest in the whole ad, right when the product message needs to register. Anchoring that scene with a face in frame would help the explanation stick.

The blurry dark transition frames around seconds six through nine lose attention across all channels before the story has built any momentum. A tighter cut to the next scene would avoid the dip entirely.

samples.title: Sintel (trailer)
samples.attribution: © copyright Blender Foundation | durian.blender.org, CC BY 3.0

report.headline: Action peak earns its response, but the desert wind-down starts too early and the logo holds too long
report.summary: The trailer builds confidently to a genuine visual peak during the flying creature sequence, where face and body responses climb to their highest points. The transition into the desert isolation shots then bleeds momentum well before the title card appears, and the logo itself lingers past the point of diminishing returns. Getting even one more face shot into the desert stretch before the title fade would hold the emotional thread longer.

moments.what_happens: The masked warrior emerges from the blizzard into a close-up.
moments.brain_response: The body and face responses jump as a human figure fills the frame for the first time. Scene-setting has handed the baton to character, and the brain follows immediately.

moments.what_happens: The elder asks 'What brings you to the land of the gatekeepers?' in tight close-up.
moments.brain_response: Hearing spikes to its single highest point in the entire trailer here. The combination of a large, detailed face and spoken dialogue locks in both social understanding and auditory processing together.

moments.what_happens: Wide shots of the ruined city give way to Sintel's wide-eyed, frightened face in close-up.
moments.brain_response: Bodies response reaches its peak across the whole clip, and faces also climbs to its highest reading. The scale contrast, creature threat, and the emotional face closeup land simultaneously, which is exactly the kind of multi-channel convergence that holds attention hard.

moments.what_happens: A lone figure crosses vast sand dunes toward the title reveal.
moments.brain_response: Bodies drops sharply into negative territory as the character shrinks to a speck. The scene is beautiful and thematically resonant for loneliness, but with the sound off the response is already below typical, meaning visuals alone are not sustaining engagement through this stretch.
moments.suggestion: Cut to a single mid-shot or close-up of Sintel's face walking before the title fades in, so the emotional thread stays open rather than closing on pure landscape.

moments.what_happens: Static SINTEL logo holds on a black background for about five seconds.
moments.brain_response: All channels continue declining through the hold. Five-plus seconds of a static logo is longer than the brain needs to register it, and the trailer's hard-won emotional build has fully dissipated by the end.
moments.suggestion: Trim the logo hold to two to three seconds max, or dissolve it over the final desert frame rather than cutting to pure black first.

strengths: The escalating creature-and-combat sequence from seconds 22 through 27 uses scale shifts and face closeups together in a way that earns the trailer's highest overall brain response.
Every face closeup in the dialogue exchange (seconds 12 to 15) is timed tightly to spoken lines, so hearing and social understanding rise together rather than taking turns.
improvements: The desert isolation sequence is striking visually but runs three to four seconds without a human face, draining body and face responses right when the trailer needs to close strong.
The logo card lingers beyond the natural attention window, so viewers coast out on a falling signal rather than on the high of the final dramatic beat.

samples.title: Big Buck Bunny (55 s excerpt)
samples.attribution: © copyright 2008, Blender Foundation | www.bigbuckbunny.org, CC BY 3.0

report.headline: Extreme close-ups earn the peak, but the apple mid-section runs long and loses steam
report.summary: The flower-sniffing and butterfly sequences drive some of the strongest body and face responses in the whole film, earned by bold framing that fills the frame with character. The apple-picking stretch from roughly seconds 28 to 37 is the one genuine valley, with overall engagement below typical and the hearing channel well below typical for nearly ten seconds straight. Trimming that static mid-shot stretch by three or four seconds would keep the arc tight before the strong final close.

moments.what_happens: Bunny presses his face into the daisies in extreme close-up.
moments.brain_response: Bodies and faces both surge well above typical here. The camera angle floods the entire frame with the character's physical form, which drives an unusually strong body-detection response that tracks right through these shots.

moments.what_happens: Bunny rolls on the grass as the butterfly lands on him.
moments.brain_response: This is the sustained peak of the whole video. Bodies hits its highest value of the film and the hearing channel is also well above typical, meaning both the action and the soundtrack are working together to hold the brain in.

moments.what_happens: Bunny stands alone in a wide mid-shot holding the apple and staring at the tree.
moments.brain_response: Overall drops below typical and hearing falls well below typical for nearly ten seconds, the longest valley in the film. The muted response stays modestly positive, so the visuals are fine, but the audio side is dragging the combined score down across this whole stretch.
moments.suggestion: Cut at least three seconds from this beat. Hold the suspicious face a beat longer, then jump straight to the throw or the smash rather than lingering in the contemplation.

moments.what_happens: Bunny reacts in close-up as the butterfly returns and lands on him, ending with 'Thank you.'
moments.brain_response: Faces, bodies, and the hearing channel all climb together through this sequence, with hearing reaching its highest point in the film at the final second. The social and speech scores also rise, confirming the emotional beat is landing well.

strengths: The willingness to hold extreme low-angle and close-up framings for several seconds pays off clearly, producing body and face responses far above what a more conventional mid-shot approach would have delivered.
The film finishes on an upward arc, with hearing and understanding both climbing through the last six seconds, so the closing emotional beat feels earned rather than trailing off.
improvements: The apple section uses a wide, static composition for too long. That framing works as punctuation but not as a ten-second hold, and the signals confirm it is the one place where the edit loses the audience.

The transitional landscape shots around seconds 42 to 43, where the character nearly leaves the frame entirely, reset the scene efficiently but also drop the body and face contact that drives the strongest responses in this film. Even a brief reaction insert would bridge the gap.

report.headline: A and B are two cuts of the same CeraVe Michael Cera campaign: A is tight and punchy, B expands the joke but opens slowly
report.summary: A is a 30-second cut that puts Michael Cera on camera from the first frame and closes with a sharp product punchline. B is a 76-second expanded version that layers in additional set pieces but spends nine seconds on curtains and silhouette before Cera's face appears. A dominates the opening; B holds attention better through its mid-section once it recovers.

differences.what_differs: A opens with Cera speaking directly to camera; B opens with curtains and a silhouetted figure.
differences.brain_response: A drives hearing and face response well above typical from the very first second. B sits well below typical across all channels for its first seven seconds because there is no recognizable face or speech to lock onto.

differences.what_differs: B includes an enchanted-garden and animated narwhal sequence not present in A.
differences.brain_response: Body and scene response stay above typical during this stretch, but speech comprehension drops below typical and overall engagement is only just above typical, so the visual spectacle earns less than the live-action Cera scenes before it.

differences.what_differs: A closes on the product jar with the 'NOT Michael Cera' title card; B closes on curtains and a plain logo.
differences.brain_response: A's understanding stays clearly above typical through the final seconds as viewers read and process the punchline. B's final seconds fall well below typical on every channel as faces, bodies, and sound all drain away on the logo card.

a_does_better: A earns strong hearing and face response from the opening frame, giving the joke instant purchase before attention can wander.
